Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verses 1–9:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat ash-Shu'ara'

This surah is entirely Meccan, so said the majority of people. Muqatil said: "Some of it is Medinan: the verse in which the poets are mentioned," and the verse of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 197].

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so that their necks would remain bowed before it.﴾ ﴿Never comes to them a new reminder from the Most Gracious, but they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

The discussion of the letters at the beginnings of the surahs has already preceded, in full.

"Tilka" is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and it together with its predicate (khabar) takes the place of the predicate of "Ta-Sin-Mim" according to some interpretations. The indication by "tilka" depends on the disagreement regarding "Ta-Sin-Mim." According to some opinions, "tilka" indicates something present, and "dhalika" indicates something existing, just as "hadhihi" may be used to indicate an absent thing that is known, as if it were present.

And ﴿the Clear Book﴾ is the Qur'an.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "Ta-Sin-Mim" with a kasra on the ta'. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha and with the idgham (assimilation) of the nun of "Sin" into the mim. Hamza alone read it with idhhar (clear pronunciation) of it, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, and it is also transmitted from Nafi'. Ya'qub transmitted from Abu Ja'far and Nafi' a pause after each letter separately. Abu Hatim said: "The preferred reading is a fatha on the ta' and idgham of the last letter of 'Sin' into the first letter of 'Mim', so the mim becomes connected."

And His saying, ﴿Perhaps you...﴾ is a consolation to Muhammad (ﷺ) for what he was experiencing of anxiety and eagerness for their faith, so that he was occupied in heart, within the realm of fear for his own self. The "bakhi'" (one who destroys himself) is the one who kills himself and destroys it through grief, so said Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and the people. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Ala ayyuha dha al-bakhi'u al-wajdu nafsahu / li-shay'in nahathathu 'an yadayhi al-maqaduru

He was addressed with "la'alla" in accordance with what is in human nature of expecting destruction in such a state. The meaning of the verse: "Do not be concerned, O Muhammad, about them, and convey your message; and it is not upon you to bring them to faith, for that is in the hand of Allah, the Exalted; had He willed, they would have believed." And His saying, "alla" is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

And His saying, ﴿If We will﴾ is a conditional clause, and the ambiguity inherent in the conditional is, in this verse, within our domain. As for Allah, the Exalted, He knows that He does not send down upon them a sign of compulsion. Rather, Allah, the Exalted, made the signs of the prophets and the signs indicating Him exposed to observation and reflection, so that whoever His knowledge has preceded in guidance would be guided, and whoever His knowledge has preceded in misguidance would go astray, and so that there would be an acquisition (taksub) in the looking by which reward and punishment are connected. A sign of compulsion would negate all of this, were it to be sent down.

He read "nunazzil" with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the zay: Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', al-A'raj, 'Asim and al-Hasan. Abu 'Amr and the people of Basra read with a sukun on the nun and a light zay. Harun transmitted from Abu 'Amr "yasha' yunazzil" with the ya' in both. The submission to the evidence in the revealed sign would be consequent upon one of two aspects: either through fear of destruction in opposing the command accompanying it, like the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel; or that it be so clear that submission to it and the yielding of souls occur. Neither of these two was brought by a prophet. The reason for this is what we have mentioned, and it is a explanation explicitly stated by the scholars. Talha read "fatazull a'naquhum", and this is what is meant in the reading of the majority; the placing of the past tense in the position of the future is an indication of strengthening the occurrence of the act.

His saying, ﴿a'naquhum﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first, which is the saying of Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash, is that it means their groups; it is said: "He came in a 'unuq of people," that is, a group. From this is the saying of the poet:

Anna al-'Iraqa wa-ahlahu / 'unuqun ilayka fa-hayta hayta

And upon this is interpreted the saying of Abu Mihjan:

.................. / wa-aktumu as-sirra fihi darbatu al-'unuqi

And for this reason it is said "'unuqu raqabatin," and it is not said "'unuqu 'unuqin," to flee from homonymy, so said al-Zahrawi.

The other interpretation is that by "a'naq" he means the well-known organ, because the bowing of the neck and the nape is the sign of humiliation and submission. From this is the saying of the poet:

Wa-idha al-rijalu ra'aw Yazida ra'aytahum / khudha al-riqabi nawakisa al-absari

So the meaning of this interpretation, we speak about His saying, ﴿khadi'in﴾: how did He make it plural in the manner of those who reason? This is explained by two styles of Arabic speech. One is that the attribution to those who reason conveyed its judgment to those who do not reason, just as attribution to a feminine noun conveys the feminine marker to a masculine one. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

................. / kama sharaqat sadra al-qanati mina al-dami

And this is common.

The other style is that "a'naq," since it is described by an act that is only intended by humans, namely submission, is treated as such, being an act that follows a matter in the soul; so it was made plural in the manner of those who reason. This is similar to His saying: ﴿We came willingly﴾ [Fussilat: 11], and His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "lahā khādi'a."

Then He rebuked the disbelievers and drew attention to the evil of their action with His saying: ﴿Never comes to them...﴾ The verse. His saying ﴿muhdath﴾ means: newness of coming, that is, the arrival of the Qur'an to mankind was one thing after another. A group said: it is possible that by "dhikr" (reminder) is meant Muhammad (ﷺ), as He said in another verse: ﴿Allah has sent down to you a reminder﴾ [al-Talaq: 10] ﴿a messenger﴾ [al-Talaq: 11], so describing him as "muhdath" is well-established.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The first opinion is more eloquent.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them...﴾ The verse is a threat of punishment in this world and the Hereafter. What strengthens that it is a threat of punishment in this world is that this has indeed befallen them, as at Badr and other events.

Since their turning away from reflection on the Creator and the God was the greatest of their disbelief, and they were making idols into gods and turning away from remembrance in this matter, He drew attention to the power of Allah, the Exalted, and that He is the Creator, the Originator who deserves worship, by His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth...﴾ The verse. "Zawj" means type and kind, and "karim" means good and perfected, so said Mujahid and Qatada. What is meant is the things by which the affairs and sustenance and plants are maintained, and this includes animals, because they too come from growth. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Al-Sha'bi said: "People are of the growth of the earth; whoever goes to Paradise is noble, and whoever ends up in the opposite of that is base."

His saying, ﴿And most of them were not believers﴾ is a judgment that most of them are disbelievers. Then He gave a warning with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾, meaning: He is mighty in His vengeance against the disbelievers, and merciful to the believers of every nation. Ibn Jurayj said something similar to this, and in the word "al-Rahim" there is a promise.

Anna al-'Iraqa wa-ahlahu / 'unuqun ilayka fa-hayta hayta

.................. / wa-aktumu as-sirra fihi darbatu al-'unuqi

And for this reason it is said "'unuqu raqabatin," and it is not said "'unuqu 'unuqin," to flee from homonymy, so said al-Zahrawi.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The first opinion is more eloquent.

[p. 472] The Exalted said:

﴿And when your Lord called out to Moses: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my chest will constrict, and my tongue will not be loosed, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "Never! Go, both of you, with Our signs. We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'We are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ ﴿He said: "Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life?﴾ ﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were among the disbelievers."﴾

The estimate (al-taqdir): "Recall when your Lord called out to Moses." The narrating of this story is an illustration for the disbelievers of Quraysh, for their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ). The *an* in His words ﴿an i'ti﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira), having no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), in the sense of *ay* ("that is"), or it may be other than that, in which case it is in the accusative position. His words ﴿Will they not fear God?﴾ mean: "Say to them." This phrase combines the negation of piety from them and the command to them to be pious.

The majority of readers recited *yattaqun* with the *ya'* (third person), while 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Hammad ibn Salama and Abu Qilaba recited *tattaqun* with the *ta'* (second person), with the meaning "say to them."

Because of the great power of Pharaoh, his claim to divinity, the length of his reign, and the awe of him that had seeped into hearts, Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, I fear that they will deny me.﴾ The majority of readers recited *wa-yadiqu* (and will constrict) and *yantaliqu* (and will be loosed) in the nominative (raf'). Al-A'raj, Talha and 'Isa recited both in the accusative (nasb). The nominative reading is a report from Moses (peace be upon him) of the occurrence of the constriction of his chest and the non-loosening of his tongue, and for this reason Abu Hatim preferred this reading. The accusative reading requires that this be included under his fear, being coordinated (ʿatf) with *yukadhdhibun* (they will deny me). There was sharpness in Moses's character (peace be upon him), and there was a speech impediment in his tongue due to the ember in his childhood. Abu 'Amr reported from al-A'raj that he recited *wa-yadiqa* in the accusative and *yantaliqu* in the nominative. Each interpretation has a side of argument. Whenever one of two disputants attains this rank, and his opponent is the opposite of it, the one characterised by it prevails, and his speech has a stronger effect on souls.

Musa (peace be upon him) answered him with attributes by which the listener clearly sees that Pharaoh has no share in them, and that they are the lordship of the heavens and the earth. This dispute from Pharaoh shows that Musa (peace be upon him) called him to monotheism. Pharaoh then said, ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ in the sense of rousing them or of wonder at the awfulness of the statement, since the belief of the people was that Pharaoh was their lord and their object of worship, and the Pharaohs before him were likewise. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 26, verses 29–37:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among those imprisoned."﴾ ﴿He said, "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and suddenly it was a clear serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and suddenly it was white for the onlookers.﴾ ﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician.﴾ ﴿He wants to expel you from your land with his magic, so what do you advise?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Postpone him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers﴾ ﴿who will bring you every knowing magician."﴾

When Pharaoh (may Allah curse him) was cut off in the matter of proof, he returned to domination and overpowering, and this is the clearest sign of being cut off. So he threatened Musa (peace be upon him) when his argument had defeated him. In his threat of imprisonment there is weakness, because his temperament had collapsed in front of him. It is reported that he used to be terrified of him to the point that he could not hold his urine. It is also reported that his prison was worse than killing, since it was in a sealed place of the earth from which he would never be released, and it was dreaded.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the tendency of the abode [... ] until today.

Musa (peace be upon him) possessed a command from Allah, blessed and exalted, by which Pharaoh's threat did not frighten him. So he said to him, in a gentle manner and hoping for his faith: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾, meaning: my truthfulness will become evident to you through it. Would you then imprison me? When Pharaoh heard this, he hoped to find in the midst of it a point of opposition, so he said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾

﴿So he threw down his staff﴾ from his hand. It was one of the staves of Paradise, the staff of Adam (peace be upon him). It is also narrated that it was made of a sprig of basil, and it was with Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) among the staves of the prophets (peace be upon them). He gave it to Musa (peace be upon him) when Musa was tending the sheep, in a form that has already been mentioned, which indicated the prophethood of Musa. It had two prongs at its head, and between them was the mouth of the serpent.

The thu'ban (serpent) is the largest of snakes. We have already mentioned in what preceded what has been reported about the size of snakes and other narrations concerning this verse.

Musa (peace be upon him) drew his hand out of his garment, and it was shining as if it were a piece of the sun. When Pharaoh saw this, it overwhelmed him, and he had no means of repelling it. Yet he resorted to calling it magic, and he hoped, because of the high standing and abundance of the science of magic at that time, that this might be a means of opposing Musa (peace be upon him). So he deluded his people and followers into thinking that Musa (peace be upon him) was a magician.

The word "ḥawlahu" (around him) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), and it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "those being around him." The element governing it is therefore omitted, while the true governing element is the circumstance itself. The one that governs the circumstance is "qāla" (he said), because it is the verb that governs the one described by the circumstance through the intermediary of the preposition lām, as in the example: "I passed by Hind laughing." (Here the circumstance is "ḍāḥikatan," and the one it describes is "Hind.")

Then he consulted them about his affair and incited them against him in his words: ﴿He wants to expel you from your land with his magic﴾. They advised him to postpone the matter of Musa and his brother and to gather magicians to oppose him. It is also reported that they advised imprisoning him. The word "al-irjā'" (postponement) in their terms means delay. They did not advise killing him, because his proof was luminous and their misguidance regarding the lordship of Pharaoh was manifest, so they feared the strife, and they hoped that he would be overcome by an argument that would persuade the common people. "Al-ḥāshir" means the one who gathers.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read ﴿bi-kulli saḥḥārin﴾ (every great magician), and it is in the intensive form (for emphasis). 'Asim and al-A'mash also read ﴿bi-kulli sāḥirin﴾ (every magician).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verse 38–44:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿So the magicians were assembled for the appointed time of a known day﴾ ﴿And it was said to the people: "Will you gather?"﴾ ﴿"So that we may follow the magicians, if they are the victors."﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will there truly be a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near."﴾ ﴿Moses said to them, "Throw down what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we are indeed the victors."﴾

The day is the Day of Adornment (yawm al-zinah). It is said that it was the day the channel of the Nile was broken, and so it became the Day of Adornment in Egypt for all time. Ibn Zayd said that this gathering took place in Alexandria.

His saying, ﴿so that we may follow the magicians﴾, does not mean that they would follow them in magic; rather, he meant something like: that we follow them in supporting our religion and our creed, and in refuting those who oppose it.

al-A'raj and Abu 'Amr read "a-inna lana" with the interrogative alif. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Shayba read "inna lana" in the affirmative. 'Isa read "na'im" with a kasra on the 'ayn.

The nearness (taqrib) that Pharaoh promised them is the rank (jah) added to the reward they had asked for, and nearness to the king, who was their god. People differed about the number of the magicians, and we have mentioned that earlier. They were gathered from the cities of Egypt and the countryside along the Nile, and those were the lands of magic, such as al-Farama and others. Most of them were from al-Farama and the mountains. The staffs were loads of camels.

His saying, ﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾, may carry two meanings. The first is an oath: it is as if they swore by the might of Pharaoh, just as you say, "By God, I will not do such and such." Their oath by the might of Pharaoh was thus not an acceptable one. The second is that it is in the way of glorifying Pharaoh, since they worshipped him, and seeking blessing through his name, as you say when you begin a task: "In the name of God," and "With the blessing of God," and similar.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 26, verses 45–51:**

The Exalted said:

﴿So Moses threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely presented.﴾ ﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ ﴿He said: "Have you believed in Him before I give you permission? He is indeed your chief who taught you magic. You will soon know. I will surely cut off your hands and feet on alternate sides, and I will crucify you all."﴾ ﴿They said: "No harm. Indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾ ﴿We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we are the first of the believers."﴾

What people have mentioned about the size of the serpent when Moses, peace be upon him, threw his staff has already been discussed in other than this surah. In this verse there is much that is omitted but indicated by the apparent meaning, and it has been mentioned in other passages: it is Moses' fear, peace be upon him, that their magic would prevail, and that they would frighten people and make people imagine, through their ropes and staves, that these were moving with intent. Then the serpent that Allah created in the staff swallowed those ropes and staves entirely, and Allah, exalted is He, caused them to vanish within its belly. The staff returned to its former state when Moses, peace be upon him, took hold of the opening that was in its head, put his hand into its mouth, and it returned to being a staff by the permission of Allah, blessed and exalted is He.

The majority of reciters read "تَلَقَّفَ" (talaqqafa), with a open tā' and lām and a shaddah on the qāf. Ḥafṣ, from 'Āṣim, read "تَلْقَفُ" (talqafu), with a sukūn on the lām and a light qāf. Al-Bazzī and Ibn Fulayḥ, from Ibn Kathīr, narrated it with a shaddah on the tā', a fatḥah on the lām and a shaddah on the qāf. According to this reading, when one begins a sentence with it, one must bring the hamzat al-waṣl (the connecting hamza, a hamza pronounced only when beginning speech and dropped in continuation), and the hamzat al-waṣl does not enter present-tense verbs, just as it does not enter active participles.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿what they had falsely presented﴾, meaning: what they lie about with it and because of it, in their claim that it was an opposition to Moses, peace be upon him, and a kind of his action. Al-ifk (falsehood) means lying.

Then, when the sorcerers saw the staff free of the craft of magic, and saw in it, after that, a matter from Allah, exalted is He, that convinced them that it was not within the power of humans, they submitted. They saw that the gain was faith and holding fast to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. So they all prostrated to Allah, exalted is He, acknowledging His oneness and His power. They reached their faith through Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and they declared that this was at their hands. For their saying: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾ means that, so they did not repeat the clarification in their saying: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ except for what we have mentioned.

When Pharaoh and the chiefs saw the faith of the sorcerers, and the proof was established by the faith of the people of their knowledge and the source of their support, Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, fell into a great predicament. So he returned to the sorcerers with this other argument, and he confronted them, rebuking them for their believing in Moses before his permission. In this expression there is a great ambiguity, because one of its possible meanings is that if they had asked his permission for that, he would have permitted it. Then he threatened them with cutting off hands and feet on alternate sides, and with crucifixion on the trunks of palm trees. They said to him: "No harm," meaning: that will not harm us, given our return to the forgiveness of Allah, exalted is He, and His pleasure. It is related that he carried out that threat against them, and crucified them on the Nile. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs in the evening." Their saying: ﴿that we are the first of the believers﴾ means: among the Copts and their followers. Otherwise, the Children of Israel had already believed. People read "أنّا" (annā), with a fatḥah on the alif, while Abān ibn Taghlib read "إنّا" (innā), with a kasrah on the alif, meaning that their hope is only on this condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verses 52–62:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers,﴾ ﴿"Indeed, these are but a small band,﴾ ﴿and indeed they have enraged us,﴾ ﴿and indeed we are a vigilant host."﴾ ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station.﴾ ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them.﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And when the two hosts sighted each other, the companions of Musa said, "Indeed, we are overtaken!"﴾ ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾

Then, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed to make manifest His command concerning the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the drowning of Pharaoh and his people, He commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to set out with the Children of Israel by night from Egypt. He informed him that they would be pursued, and commanded him to head towards the sea. He also commanded that the Children of Israel should borrow the jewelry and property of the Copts and take as much of their wealth as they could. This is what some commentators (mufassirun) have related. He also commanded him to take provisions for the journey, so he was told to take fatir (unleavened bread), since it keeps longer and is more durable. It is related that the haste of their departure prevented them from preparing provisions. Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel before dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and turned towards the sea. A man of the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, and Musa, peace be upon him, would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Musa's night journey with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt for the troops to catch up with him. It is related that he overtook them with six hundred thousand dark-colored horses, apart from the horses of other colors. It is also related that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said this, and Allah knows best its authenticity. What is definitively necessary from the verse is that Musa, peace be upon him, went out with a great host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of horsemen."

As for "al-shirdhima" (the small band): it is a small, despised group. The shirdhima of anything is its base remnant. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Diligent among the shara dhim of sandals"

Another poet said:

"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn out,
shreds (shara dhim) at which the one who longs for warmth laughs."

As for His words, "la-ghaʾiẓūn" (enraging us): it means that they opposed the command, took the property as a loan, and fled from them that night, as has been related. Abu Hatim said: "One who is not relied upon recited: [lashirdhimatun qalīlūn], but this is not transmitted as a valid reading."

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "ḥadhirūn" (wary), the plural of "ḥadhir," which denotes one who is naturally disposed to caution. Here it is not an active participle governing an object. The same usage occurs in the verse of Abu Ahmar:

"Can I be postponed to another day? Indeed I am ḥawālī (protected) and indeed I am ḥadhir (wary)."

Scholars differ over whether the form fa'il (ḥadhir) functions as an active verb. Sibawayh said that it does, and recited:

"Wary of matters that will not harm him, and secure from what does not save him from the decrees."

Al-Lahiqi claimed that this verse was falsely attributed to Sibawayh. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ḥādhirūn" (vigilant), which is the one who has taken to caution. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I am vigilant, sharpening my weapon, against the joints of a fierce, skillful warrior."

Ibn Abi 'Imara and Sumayt ibn 'Ajlan recited "ḥādirūn" with an undotted dal, from the expression "'ayn ḥadhra," meaning "full." The meaning is then: "full of rage and disdain."

The pronoun in His words, "fa-akhrajnāhum" (So We expelled them), refers to the Copts. "The gardens and springs" are on the two banks of the Nile from Aswan to Rashid. This was said by Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others. As for "the treasures," it has been said that they refer to the wealth which they had squandered; Mujahid said: "Because they never spent it in obedience." It has also been said that they refer to the treasures of al-Muqattam and its mines, which remain to this day. As for "the noble station," Ibn Lahi'a said: it is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that it refers to the pulpits, and that it refers to the assemblies of rulers and judges. Al-Hasan said: the fine assemblies. Al-A'raj and Qatada recited "aqāmi" with a damma on the mim, from "aqāma" (to establish).

The inheritance of the Children of Israel admits of two meanings: one is that Allah made them inherit this shore (ḍifa) of the land of Syria; the other is that He made them inherit Egypt, but only after a long period of time. Al-Hasan said this, although the histories do not record that the Children of Israel ruled Egypt. The word "mushriqīn" means: at the rising of the sun, that is, when they entered into it. It has also been said that it means: towards the east. Al-Hasan recited "fa-ittaba'ūhum" with an elongated alif and a doubled ta'.

When Pharaoh caught up with his host, and reached Musa, peace be upon him, and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the powerful enemy behind them and the sea before them, their assumptions became evil, and they said to Musa, peace be upon him, in a tone of reproach and rudeness: "Indeed, we are overtaken!" That is: "This is your way of acting." He answered their statement, rebuked them, and mentioned the promise of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to him of guidance and victory. The majority recited "Innā la-mudrakūn," while al-A'raj and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited "Innā la-mudarrakūn," with a doubled dal and a fatha on the ra, meaning: "We are being pursued continuously until we are annihilated." Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "tarī'a al-jam'ān" with a kasra on the ra, with a long vowel and then a hamza. This is also related from 'Asim, and it is also related from him with a fatha and a long vowel. The majority recite it like "tarā'ā" [p. 486], and this is the correct reading, because it is of the form tafā'ul. Abu Hatim said: "The reading of Hamza in this word is impossible," and he rejected it, saying: "What is related from Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash is an error."

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers,﴾ ﴿"Indeed, these are but a small band,﴾ ﴿and indeed they have enraged us,﴾ ﴿and indeed we are a vigilant host."﴾ ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station.﴾ ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them.﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And when the two hosts sighted each other, the companions of Musa said, "Indeed, we are overtaken!"﴾ ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾

Then, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed to make manifest His command concerning the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the drowning of Pharaoh and his people, He commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to set out with the Children of Israel by night from Egypt. He informed him that they would be pursued, and commanded him to head towards the sea. He also commanded that the Children of Israel should borrow the jewelry and property of the Copts and take as much of their wealth as they could. This is what some commentators (mufassirun) have related. He also commanded him to take provisions for the journey, so he was told to take fatir (unleavened bread), since it keeps longer and is more durable. It is related that the haste of their departure prevented them from preparing provisions. Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel before dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and turned towards the sea. A man of the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, and Musa, peace be upon him, would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Musa's night journey with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt for the troops to catch up with him. It is related that he overtook them with six hundred thousand dark-colored horses, apart from the horses of other colors. It is also related that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said this, and Allah knows best its authenticity. What is definitively necessary from the verse is that Musa, peace be upon him, went out with a great host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of horsemen."

As for "al-shirdhima" (the small band): it is a small, despised group. The shirdhima of anything is its base remnant. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Diligent among the shara dhim of sandals"

Another poet said:

"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn out,
shreds (shara dhim) at which the one who longs for warmth laughs."

As for His words, "la-ghaʾiẓūn" (enraging us): it means that they opposed the command, took the property as a loan, and fled from them that night, as has been related. Abu Hatim said: "One who is not relied upon recited: [lashirdhimatun qalīlūn], but this is not transmitted as a valid reading."

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "ḥadhirūn" (wary), the plural of "ḥadhir," which denotes one who is naturally disposed to caution. Here it is not an active participle governing an object. The same usage occurs in the verse of Abu Ahmar:

"Can I be postponed to another day? Indeed I am ḥawālī (protected) and indeed I am ḥadhir (wary)."

Scholars differ over whether the form fa'il (ḥadhir) functions as an active verb. Sibawayh said that it does, and recited:

"Wary of matters that will not harm him, and secure from what does not save him from the decrees."

Al-Lahiqi claimed that this verse was falsely attributed to Sibawayh. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ḥādhirūn" (vigilant), which is the one who has taken to caution. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I am vigilant, sharpening my weapon, against the joints of a fierce, skillful warrior."

Ibn Abi 'Imara and Sumayt ibn 'Ajlan recited "ḥādirūn" with an undotted dal, from the expression "'ayn ḥadhra," meaning "full." The meaning is then: "full of rage and disdain."

The pronoun in His words, "fa-akhrajnāhum" (So We expelled them), refers to the Copts. "The gardens and springs" are on the two banks of the Nile from Aswan to Rashid. This was said by Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others. As for "the treasures," it has been said that they refer to the wealth which they had squandered; Mujahid said: "Because they never spent it in obedience." It has also been said that they refer to the treasures of al-Muqattam and its mines, which remain to this day. As for "the noble station," Ibn Lahi'a said: it is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that it refers to the pulpits, and that it refers to the assemblies of rulers and judges. Al-Hasan said: the fine assemblies. Al-A'raj and Qatada recited "aqāmi" with a damma on the mim, from "aqāma" (to establish).

The inheritance of the Children of Israel admits of two meanings: one is that Allah made them inherit this shore (ḍifa) of the land of Syria; the other is that He made them inherit Egypt, but only after a long period of time. Al-Hasan said this, although the histories do not record that the Children of Israel ruled Egypt. The word "mushriqīn" means: at the rising of the sun, that is, when they entered into it. It has also been said that it means: towards the east. Al-Hasan recited "fa-ittaba'ūhum" with an elongated alif and a doubled ta'.

When Pharaoh caught up with his host, and reached Musa, peace be upon him, and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the powerful enemy behind them and the sea before them, their assumptions became evil, and they said to Musa, peace be upon him, in a tone of reproach and rudeness: "Indeed, we are overtaken!" That is: "This is your way of acting." He answered their statement, rebuked them, and mentioned the promise of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to him of guidance and victory. The majority recited "Innā la-mudrakūn," while al-A'raj and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited "Innā la-mudarrakūn," with a doubled dal and a fatha on the ra, meaning: "We are being pursued continuously until we are annihilated." Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "tarī'a al-jam'ān" with a kasra on the ra, with a long vowel and then a hamza. This is also related from 'Asim, and it is also related from him with a fatha and a long vowel. The majority recite it like "tarā'ā" [p. 486], and this is the correct reading, because it is of the form tafā'ul. Abu Hatim said: "The reading of Hamza in this word is impossible," and he rejected it, saying: "What is related from Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash is an error."

Then, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed to make manifest His command concerning the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the drowning of Pharaoh and his people, He commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to set out with the Children of Israel by night from Egypt. He informed him that they would be pursued, and commanded him to head towards the sea. He also commanded that the Children of Israel should borrow the jewelry and property of the Copts and take as much of their wealth as they could. This is what some commentators (mufassirun) have related. He also commanded him to take provisions for the journey, so he was told to take fatir (unleavened bread), since it keeps longer and is more durable. It is related that the haste of their departure prevented them from preparing provisions. Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel before dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and turned towards the sea. A man of the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, and Musa, peace be upon him, would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Musa's night journey with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt for the troops to catch up with him. It is related that he overtook them with six hundred thousand dark-colored horses, apart from the horses of other colors. It is also related that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said this, and Allah knows best its authenticity. What is definitively necessary from the verse is that Musa, peace be upon him, went out with a great host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of horsemen."

As for "al-shirdhima" (the small band): it is a small, despised group. The shirdhima of anything is its base remnant. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Diligent among the shara dhim of sandals"

Another poet said:

"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn out,
shreds (shara dhim) at which the one who longs for warmth laughs."

As for His words, "la-ghaʾiẓūn" (enraging us): it means that they opposed the command, took the property as a loan, and fled from them that night, as has been related. Abu Hatim said: "One who is not relied upon recited: [lashirdhimatun qalīlūn], but this is not transmitted as a valid reading."

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "ḥadhirūn" (wary), the plural of "ḥadhir," which denotes one who is naturally disposed to caution. Here it is not an active participle governing an object. The same usage occurs in the verse of Abu Ahmar:

"Can I be postponed to another day? Indeed I am ḥawālī (protected) and indeed I am ḥadhir (wary)."

Scholars differ over whether the form fa'il (ḥadhir) functions as an active verb. Sibawayh said that it does, and recited:

"Wary of matters that will not harm him, and secure from what does not save him from the decrees."

Al-Lahiqi claimed that this verse was falsely attributed to Sibawayh. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ḥādhirūn" (vigilant), which is the one who has taken to caution. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I am vigilant, sharpening my weapon, against the joints of a fierce, skillful warrior."

Ibn Abi 'Imara and Sumayt ibn 'Ajlan recited "ḥādirūn" with an undotted dal, from the expression "'ayn ḥadhra," meaning "full." The meaning is then: "full of rage and disdain."

The pronoun in His words, "fa-akhrajnāhum" (So We expelled them), refers to the Copts. "The gardens and springs" are on the two banks of the Nile from Aswan to Rashid. This was said by Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others. As for "the treasures," it has been said that they refer to the wealth which they had squandered; Mujahid said: "Because they never spent it in obedience." It has also been said that they refer to the treasures of al-Muqattam and its mines, which remain to this day. As for "the noble station," Ibn Lahi'a said: it is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that it refers to the pulpits, and that it refers to the assemblies of rulers and judges. Al-Hasan said: the fine assemblies. Al-A'raj and Qatada recited "aqāmi" with a damma on the mim, from "aqāma" (to establish).

The inheritance of the Children of Israel admits of two meanings: one is that Allah made them inherit this shore (ḍifa) of the land of Syria; the other is that He made them inherit Egypt, but only after a long period of time. Al-Hasan said this, although the histories do not record that the Children of Israel ruled Egypt. The word "mushriqīn" means: at the rising of the sun, that is, when they entered into it. It has also been said that it means: towards the east. Al-Hasan recited "fa-ittaba'ūhum" with an elongated alif and a doubled ta'.

When Pharaoh caught up with his host, and reached Musa, peace be upon him, and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the powerful enemy behind them and the sea before them, their assumptions became evil, and they said to Musa, peace be upon him, in a tone of reproach and rudeness: "Indeed, we are overtaken!" That is: "This is your way of acting." He answered their statement, rebuked them, and mentioned the promise of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to him of guidance and victory. The majority recited "Innā la-mudrakūn," while al-A'raj and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited "Innā la-mudarrakūn," with a doubled dal and a fatha on the ra, meaning: "We are being pursued continuously until we are annihilated." Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "tarī'a al-jam'ān" with a kasra on the ra, with a long vowel and then a hamza. This is also related from 'Asim, and it is also related from him with a fatha and a long vowel. The majority recite it like "tarā'ā" [p. 486], and this is the correct reading, because it is of the form tafā'ul. Abu Hatim said: "The reading of Hamza in this word is impossible," and he rejected it, saying: "What is related from Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash is an error."

﴿فَأوحَيْنا إلى مُوسى أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ البَحْرَ فانْفَلَقَ فَكانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كالطَوْدِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ﴿وَأزْلَفْنا ثَمَّ الآخَرِينَ﴾ ﴿وَأنْجَيْنا مُوسى ومَن مَعَهُ أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿ثُمَّ أغْرَقْنا الآخَرِينَ﴾ ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لآيَةً وما كانَ أكْثَرُهم مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ﴿وَإنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهو العَزِيزُ الرَحِيمُ﴾

["And We revealed to Moses: Strike the sea with your staff. So it parted, and each part was like a great mountain. And We brought near the others there. And We saved Moses and all who were with him. Then We drowned the others. Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful."]

When the affliction upon the Children of Israel became great, God, blessed and exalted, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign be connected to Moses, peace be upon him, and tied to an act that he performed. Otherwise, striking with the staff does not by itself split the sea or cause its splitting, except by what was accompanied by God's power and His origination (ikhtira'). When it split, there appeared in it twelve paths, according to the number of the tribes (asbat) of the Children of Israel, and the water stood still like a great mountain. Al-tawd means the mountain. It is related from Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others that each group among them thought that the other had drowned, so God commanded the water and it became like arches (tiqan), and some of them saw one another and were consoled.

"Wa-azlafna" means: We brought near. It is also recited with the qaf (zalafna), which Abu al-Fath attributed to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa recited "wa-zulifna" without an alif. This is because Pharaoh, may God curse him, when he reached the sea and the Children of Israel had entered it, it is said that he was resolute and said to his people: "It only split by my command," so he entered upon that. It is also said: rather, he hesitated and intended to turn back, so Gabriel, peace be upon him, appeared to him on a dark mare (fars wadiq), and he went after her, and Pharaoh's horse followed, and he entered in a similar manner and the people followed him. It is related that God made angels drive his people until they gathered them into the sea. Then Moses, peace be upon him, and his people came out onto the land through those paths. When they perceived the pursuit of Pharaoh and his people, they feared that they would come out behind them, so Moses, peace be upon him, intended to strike the sea again to rejoin it. Then it was said to him: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾ [al-Dukhan: 24]. When Pharaoh's army had fully gathered, he being their vanguard in going out, the sea closed over them and they drowned. Moses, peace be upon him, had entered the sea crosswise and came out on the bank from which he had entered, after a distance. That was on the day of 'Ashura (the tenth of Muharram). Al-Naqqash said: The sea that split for Moses, peace be upon him, was the Nile.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is rejected, God willing.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is an alert to the place of lesson. His saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ means: He is Mighty in His vengeance against the disbelievers, and Merciful to the believers of the community. Much of what pertains to the story of Moses, peace be upon him, has already passed.

Then We drowned the others. Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful."]

When the affliction upon the Children of Israel became great, God, blessed and exalted, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign be connected to Moses, peace be upon him, and tied to an act that he performed. Otherwise, striking with the staff does not by itself split the sea or cause its splitting, except by what was accompanied by God's power and His origination (ikhtira'). When it split, there appeared in it twelve paths, according to the number of the tribes (asbat) of the Children of Israel, and the water stood still like a great mountain. Al-tawd means the mountain. It is related from Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others that each group among them thought that the other had drowned, so God commanded the water and it became like arches (tiqan), and some of them saw one another and were consoled.

"Wa-azlafna" means: We brought near. It is also recited with the qaf (zalafna), which Abu al-Fath attributed to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa recited "wa-zulifna" without an alif. This is because Pharaoh, may God curse him, when he reached the sea and the Children of Israel had entered it, it is said that he was resolute and said to his people: "It only split by my command," so he entered upon that. It is also said: rather, he hesitated and intended to turn back, so Gabriel, peace be upon him, appeared to him on a dark mare (fars wadiq), and he went after her, and Pharaoh's horse followed, and he entered in a similar manner and the people followed him. It is related that God made angels drive his people until they gathered them into the sea. Then Moses, peace be upon him, and his people came out onto the land through those paths. When they perceived the pursuit of Pharaoh and his people, they feared that they would come out behind them, so Moses, peace be upon him, intended to strike the sea again to rejoin it. Then it was said to him: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾ [al-Dukhan: 24]. When Pharaoh's army had fully gathered, he being their vanguard in going out, the sea closed over them and they drowned. Moses, peace be upon him, had entered the sea crosswise and came out on the bank from which he had entered, after a distance. That was on the day of 'Ashura (the tenth of Muharram). Al-Naqqash said: The sea that split for Moses, peace be upon him, was the Nile.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is rejected, God willing.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is an alert to the place of lesson. His saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ means: He is Mighty in His vengeance against the disbelievers, and Merciful to the believers of the community. Much of what pertains to the story of Moses, peace be upon him, has already passed.

(p-٤٨٨)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verses 69–77:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham﴾ ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do they hear you when you call [upon them]?"﴾ ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus."﴾ ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your forefathers, the predecessors?﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds."﴾

This story includes informing of the unseen and bringing what establishes that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not know it. Then there appeared upon his tongue, in this matter, what is in the earlier Books. This verse is not an example for the Quraysh except regarding the matter of the idols alone, because there is in it no denial and punishment.

The saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, ﴿What is it that you worship?﴾ is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation (taqrir). A ṣanam (idol) is that among the idols which is in the form of a son of Adam; it was of stone, or wood, or other than that. And "ẓalla" (to remain, to continue) is customarily used for doing a thing by day, and "bāta" (to spend the night) is customarily used for doing it by night, while "ṭafiqa" is general for both aspects. However, "ẓall" may come in the sense of generality, and this place is of that kind. And "al-'ukūf" means persistence/adherence, and from it comes "al-mu'takif" (one who observes seclusion), and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

﴿...................﴾ "The Nabateans stayed devoted, playing at the Fanzaj."

Then Abraham, peace be upon him, began to make them stand upon matters which the intellect bears witness are far from the attribute of the Deity. The majority of readers recited "yasma'ūnakum" with a fatha on the ya'; Qatada recited it with a damma on it and a kasra on the mim, from asma'a (to cause to hear), and the object in this reading is omitted. The majority of reciters recited "idh tad'ūn" with the assimilation of the dal into the ta' after transposition (qalb), and it is permissible in it, by analogy, "mudhakkar," but no one recited with it; the analogical form would be to pronounce it "idh iddu'ūn" [sic: "idh dadʿūn"], and what prevented this pronunciation is the joining of the original dal in the verb, so the similarities multiplied.

And their saying: ﴿Rather, we found our fathers doing thus﴾ is the most ugly form of taqlid (blind imitation), because it is upon misguidance and in a matter whose opposite is clear and whose importance is great. So when they declared to Abraham, peace be upon him, about the greatness of that and their not reflecting, and that they had no proof, he addressed them with his disavowal of all that was worshipped besides Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, and his enmity towards it, and he expressed his hatred and rejection of every object of worship other than Allah, may He be exalted, by "enmity," since it entails dissociation. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, because idols do not feel enmity; rather, it is he who is hostile to them. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾ — one group said: it is an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil), because among the earlier forefathers there were those who worshipped besides Allah, may He be blessed and exalted. Another group said: it is an exception of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), because he only intended the worship of idols by every generation of them. And the word "'aduww" (enemy) applies to the plural, the singular, and the feminine.

﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me.﴾ ﴿And He who feeds me and gives me drink.﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.﴾ ﴿And He who causes me to die, then gives me life.﴾ ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgement.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.﴾ ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ ﴿And make me one of the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray.﴾ ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are raised.﴾

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, praised Allah, exalted is He, with these attributes by which Allah, exalted is He, has described Himself, and the one who possesses them deserves the active attributes that are particular to humans. ﴿He who created me﴾ by His power ﴿and it is He who guides me﴾, i.e., He guides me to His obedience. The words of the Mighty and Majestic ﴿feeds me and gives me drink﴾ are a renewal of the blessing of provision. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said in the book of al-Tha'labi: the meaning is: He feeds me without food, and gives me drink without drink, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed I spend the night with my Lord, who feeds me and gives me drink." Ibrahim, peace be upon him, attributed the illness to himself and the cure to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and this is the beauty of manners in speech, while all is from Allah. This is like the saying of al-Khidr, peace be upon him: ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79]. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: when I fall ill through sins, He cures me through repentance.

The majority read these verbs: [yahdini, yasqini, yashfini – yuhyini] without a yā' (ya', the final long vowel), while Nafi' and Ibn Ishaq read "yahdini" with a yā', and likewise what follows it.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, restricted himself to hoping for forgiveness, and this is evidence of the intensity of his fear despite his station and his close friendship (khullah) with Allah. His words "my sin" (khati'ati): most exegetes held that he meant his three lies: his saying "She is my sister" concerning Sarah, his saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying ﴿Rather, this one among them did it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63]. Another group said that by "sin" he meant the generic noun, which he assigned to all his affairs without specifying.

The author Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is more apparent to me, because those three have been interpreted by many scholars as ma'arid (indirect, allusive speech). Although they are lies by the ruling of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not lie except three lies," and by the ruling of what is in the hadith of intercession concerning his words about Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "Myself, myself," and he mentioned his lies, they were for the sake of benefits and support of the sharia and truth. The majority read "khati'ati" in the singular, while al-Hasan read "khataya-ya" in the plural.

The "wisdom" (hukm) for which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, supplicated is wisdom (hikmah) and prophethood, and Ibrahim's supplication in such matters carries the sense of steadfastness and continuance. His "joining with the righteous" means granting him success in an action that places him within their number or gathers him with them in Paradise, and the Blessed and Exalted answered him when He said: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 122]. The "tongue of truthfulness" is praise and the perpetuation of standing, by the consensus of the exegetes, and in the same way Allah answered his supplication, so every religion holds fast to him and esteems him, and he is upon the hanifiyyah (primordial monotheism) with which Muhammad ﷺ came. Makki said: it was also said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands for the truth, and so the supplication was answered in Muhammad ﷺ.

The author Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the language.

When he finished with the desires of this world, he sought the felicity of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss, and he likened it to what is inherited, as the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We cause to inherit from Our servants those who were pious﴾ [Maryam: 63]. His seeking forgiveness for his father in this verse came before it became clear to him, through his father's death in disbelief, that he was an enemy of Allah, i.e., decreed upon him, and this refers to the promise mentioned. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "wa-ghfir li-abawayya innahuma kana mina al-dallin" (and forgive my two parents, for they were among the astray).

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾ may be from khizy, which is humiliation, or from khaza'ah, which is shame. The pronoun in "yub'athun" (they are raised) refers to the servants, since it is known, or refers to the astray, in which case it is part of the supplication for forgiveness.

"The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit," "except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart," "and Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing," "and Hellfire will be made apparent for the deviators," "and it will be said to them: Where is that which you used to worship," "besides Allah? Can they help you, or defend themselves?" "So they will be thrown headlong into it, they and the deviators," "and the hosts of Iblis, all of them."

"Yawma" (the Day) is a substitute (badal) for the first "yawm" in His words, the Exalted: ﴿the Day when they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87]. The meaning is: the Day when the attachments of this world and its adornments will not benefit, and by this He intends the great and most comprehensive mention, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. Apparently the exception (istithna') is disconnected (munqati'), meaning: but whoever comes to Allah with a sound heart, the soundness of his heart will benefit him. His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾ mean: free from shirk and sins, and having left behind worldly attachments, even if they were permissible, such as wealth and children. Sufyan said: it is the one who meets his Lord and there is nothing in his heart other than Him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This implies the generality of the expression, but the soundness free from shirk is the most important. Al-Junayd said: "with a heart that has been stung (ladigh) by the fear of Allah." And "al-salim" (the sound) means "al-ladigh" (the one stung).

"Wa uzlifat" means: it was brought near. "Al-ghawun" (the deviators), to whom Hellfire is made apparent, are the polytheists, as evidenced by the fact that they were addressed concerning the idols. The saying to them: ﴿Where is that which you used to worship﴾ ﴿besides Allah﴾ is in the manner of reproach, rebuke and admonition for their failure to consider Him. Al-A'mash read "fa-barazat" with a fa', while the majority read it with a waw. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-baraza" with a fatha on the ba' and without doubling, with "al-jahim" in the nominative.

Then He informed about the state of the Day of Resurrection, that the idols will be "tukabkabu" in the Fire, meaning they will be cast down in one heap. He joined to them the pronoun of those who have reason, since they were mentioned in connection with worship, and actions of those who have reason were attributed to them. The pronoun in His words "hum" returns to the disbelievers, and "al-ghawun" are the devils. "Kubkiba" is the intensive form (mudaʻʻaf) of "kabba," this is the view of the majority and it is the correct one, because their meaning is one and the intensification is clear, like "sarra" and "sarsara," and other examples. "Al-ghawun" are the disbelievers encompassed by misguidance. "Junud Iblis" (the hosts of Iblis) are his offspring and everyone who followed him, because they are his troops and helpers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verse 105–122:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Noah said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿They said, "Shall we believe you, when the lowest-ranked have followed you?"﴾ ﴿He said, "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?"﴾ ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive.﴾ ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers.﴾ ﴿I am only a clear warner.﴾ ﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my people have denied me.﴾ ﴿So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment and save me and the believers who are with me."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the remaining ones afterward.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

He attributed "kadhdhabat" (denied) to "al-qawm" (the people), and in this there is no feminine marking, because "al-qawm" carries the meaning of a nation and a group. His saying "al-mursalin" (the messengers) is because whoever denies one prophet has denied all the prophets, since their message is one, their call is the same. His saying the Exalted: ﴿akhuhum﴾ (their brother) means in lineage and upbringing, not in religion. And "amin" (trustworthy) means: trusted concerning the revelation of Allah the Exalted and His message; he means in upbringing.

Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "ajri" (my reward) with a sukun on the yā' (ya), while Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shayba read it with a fatha on the yā' throughout the Qur'an. Then he returned the matter to them with the command to piety and the call to obedience, as warning, admonition and concern for them. Their nobles then turned to belittling his followers because of the lowly people and weaklings who followed him. This was like the behaviour of the Quraysh towards 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb and others. Some people said: "al-aradhilun" (the lowest-ranked) are the weavers, the cuppers and the cobblers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is by way of example, that is, people of base trades, not that these mentioned trades were specifically singled out. "Al-aradhilun" is the plural of "al-ardhal," and it is not used except definite, or in construct, or with "man." It appears from the verse that the intent of Noah's people in attributing baseness to the believers was to disparage their actions, not to look at their trades. This is indicated by Noah's saying: ﴿wa ma 'ilmi﴾ (and what is my knowledge), because the meaning of his speech is: in my view and knowledge, their deeds and beliefs hold no benefit; rather I am satisfied with their outward appearance and content myself with it, and their reckoning is upon Allah, blessed and exalted. This is similar to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say there is no god but Allah..." the hadith in its entirety.

The majority of people read "wa-attaba'aka" (and those who followed you) as a past verb. Ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani and Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Ansari read "wa-atba'uka" (and your followers) as a plural. Abu al-Fath attributed this to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Talha. Abu 'Amr said: it is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-A'mash and Abu Haywa. 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Hamadhani read "law yash'uruna" (if they could perceive) with the yā' of the third person, while the majority read "tash'urun" (you perceive) with the tā' of address. As for the grammatical analysis of His saying "wa-atba'uka": either he made it in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or it is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying ﴿anu'minu laka﴾ (shall we believe you), and that conjunction is made acceptable by the separation with "laka" (for you).

His saying ﴿min al-marjumin﴾ (among those stoned) may mean: with stones, and it may mean: with abuse and the like, which resembles stoning with stones, and it is of the stoning by the unseen and by conjecture and the like. His saying "iftah" (judge) means: decide; and "al-fattah" means the judge in a Yemeni dialect. "Al-fulk" is the ship, and its plural is also "fulk," and the discussion of this plural has already been expounded in Surat al-A'raf. "Al-mashhun" means: filled with what befits it of the amount it carries. The rest of the verse is clear.

﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Noah said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿They said, "Shall we believe you, when the lowest-ranked have followed you?"﴾ ﴿He said, "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?"﴾ ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive.﴾ ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers.﴾ ﴿I am only a clear warner.﴾ ﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my people have denied me.﴾ ﴿So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment and save me and the believers who are with me."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the remaining ones afterward.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

He attributed "kadhdhabat" (denied) to "al-qawm" (the people), and in this there is no feminine marking, because "al-qawm" carries the meaning of a nation and a group. His saying "al-mursalin" (the messengers) is because whoever denies one prophet has denied all the prophets, since their message is one, their call is the same. His saying the Exalted: ﴿akhuhum﴾ (their brother) means in lineage and upbringing, not in religion. And "amin" (trustworthy) means: trusted concerning the revelation of Allah the Exalted and His message; he means in upbringing.

Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "ajri" (my reward) with a sukun on the yā' (ya), while Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shayba read it with a fatha on the yā' throughout the Qur'an. Then he returned the matter to them with the command to piety and the call to obedience, as warning, admonition and concern for them. Their nobles then turned to belittling his followers because of the lowly people and weaklings who followed him. This was like the behaviour of the Quraysh towards 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb and others. Some people said: "al-aradhilun" (the lowest-ranked) are the weavers, the cuppers and the cobblers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is by way of example, that is, people of base trades, not that these mentioned trades were specifically singled out. "Al-aradhilun" is the plural of "al-ardhal," and it is not used except definite, or in construct, or with "man." It appears from the verse that the intent of Noah's people in attributing baseness to the believers was to disparage their actions, not to look at their trades. This is indicated by Noah's saying: ﴿wa ma 'ilmi﴾ (and what is my knowledge), because the meaning of his speech is: in my view and knowledge, their deeds and beliefs hold no benefit; rather I am satisfied with their outward appearance and content myself with it, and their reckoning is upon Allah, blessed and exalted. This is similar to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say there is no god but Allah..." the hadith in its entirety.

The majority of people read "wa-attaba'aka" (and those who followed you) as a past verb. Ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani and Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Ansari read "wa-atba'uka" (and your followers) as a plural. Abu al-Fath attributed this to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Talha. Abu 'Amr said: it is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-A'mash and Abu Haywa. 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Hamadhani read "law yash'uruna" (if they could perceive) with the yā' of the third person, while the majority read "tash'urun" (you perceive) with the tā' of address. As for the grammatical analysis of His saying "wa-atba'uka": either he made it in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or it is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying ﴿anu'minu laka﴾ (shall we believe you), and that conjunction is made acceptable by the separation with "laka" (for you).

His saying ﴿min al-marjumin﴾ (among those stoned) may mean: with stones, and it may mean: with abuse and the like, which resembles stoning with stones, and it is of the stoning by the unseen and by conjecture and the like.
