﴿The people of ʿĀd denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Hūd said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Do you build on every elevated place a landmark, playing?﴾ ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever.﴾ ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And fear Allah, who has provided you with what you know.﴾ ﴿He provided you with livestock and sons,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿They said, "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.﴾ ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the former peoples,﴾ ﴿and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

ʿĀd: a tribe, and it is treated as not inflected (diptotic) for lightness; it is said that it is the name of their father. Hūd (peace be upon him) addressed them in the same manner as all the messengers, then spoke to them about the particular actions they engaged in, which their works demanded, saying: ﴿Do you build…﴾ in the manner of reproach. "Rī'" (ريع): the elevated part of the land. From it is the saying of al-Musayyib ibn ʿAlas describing a road:

؎ In the mirage, which lowers it and raises it, a rīʿ appears like a white garment (saḥl).

And "saḥl" is a white garment.

From it is also the saying of Dhū al-Rummah:

؎ Its wing-feathers in flight, shining above a rīʿa, the dew of its night glistening on its plumage.

From it is also the saying of al-Aʿshā:

؎ And a desolate wilderness I crossed, when its mirages ran over its rīʿ.

It is said "rīʿ" with a kasra on the rāʾ, and it is said "rayʿ" with a fatḥa on it, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla recited with it. Some of the exegetes explained "rīʿ" as "the road," some as "the wide pass," and some as "the small hill."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The sum of it is that it is a conspicuous place, the one people compete over in its appearance. And "āya" (آية): the building. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: it is a landmark. Mujāhid said: pigeon-towers. Al-Naqqāsh and others said: tall palaces. "Maṣāniʿ" (مصانع): the plural of maṣnaʿ, which is what is fashioned and perfected in its construction, such as a lofty palace or the like. Qatādah said: they are water-reservoirs. As for His saying ﴿la-ʿallakum takhludūn﴾ (perhaps you will abide forever), it may mean: according to your hopes and expectations, or it may be an interrogative meaning reproach and mockery directed at them. The majority recited "takhludūn" with a fatḥa on the tā' and a ḍammah on the lām. Qatādah recited "tukhladūn" with a ḍammah on the tā' and a fatḥa on the lām; it is said: khallada al-shay' and akhladahu (someone else made it abide). Ubayy and ʿAlqamah recited "la-ʿallakum tukhallidūn" with a ḍammah on the tā', a fatḥa on the khā', a fatḥa on the lām, and a shaddah. It is reported from Ubayy: "ka'annakum takhludūn," and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: "ka'annakum takhludūn."

"Baṭsh" (البطش): seizing with force and speed. "Jabbār" (جبار): the arrogant. From it is the saying "a jabbāra palm," when it does not reach any height. From it is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the woman who refused to be moved out of his path: "She is a jabbāra." From it is also "jabarūt." So the meaning is: you are men of intense anger, possessing excessive assaults and sudden outbursts without deliberation.

Then he (peace be upon him) reminded them of Allah's favours upon them, in what He granted them of livestock, offspring, gardens, and flowing waters within them. Then he warned them of the punishment of Allah the Exalted in this world. Their reply was to equate his admonition and his abstention from admonishing. Ibn Muḥayṣin recited "waʿaẓta" with the idghām of the ẓāʾ into the tāʾ. Then they said: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the former peoples.﴾ The readers differed on this. Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn ʿĀmir recited "khuluqu" with a ḍammah on the lām, so the reference of "hādhā" is to their religion, their worship, and their handling of the buildings; that is: this which we are upon is the custom and practice of people, and there is no resurrection or punishment after it, as you claim. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Qilābah recited "khuluq" with a ḍammah on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām, and al-Aṣmaʿī transmitted it from Nāfiʿ. Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAmr recited "khalqu al-awwalīn" with a fatḥa on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām, and this is the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlqamah, and al-Ḥasan. This admits two meanings: first, that what you claim is nothing but the fabrication (ikhtilāq) of the former liars before you, so you are upon their path. Second, that they meant: this structure in which we are is nothing but the structure upon which the former people were, life and death, and there is no resurrection or punishment. Each of the meanings I have mentioned is admitted by the reading "khuluq." ʿAlqamah transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd: "in hādhā illā ikhtilāq al-awwalīn." The rest of the verse has already been explained.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verses 141–159:

The Exalted said:

﴿Thamud denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Salih said to them: "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft?﴾ ﴿And you carve out homes from the mountains, skillfully.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant,﴾ ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ ﴿They said: "You are only one of those bewitched.﴾ ﴿You are only a human like us, so bring a sign if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of a known day.﴾ ﴿Do not touch her with harm, lest the punishment of a tremendous day seize you."﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, and so they became regretful.﴾ ﴿Then the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

"Thamud": an Arab tribe. It is read both with and without tanwin (nunation), depending on whether the intended meaning is the clan or the tribe. It was recited in both ways: the majority read it without tanwin, while Ibn Wathhab and others read it with tanwin. "Salih" was their brother by lineage. The prophets from among the Arabs are four: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, and Muhammad (ﷺ), may God's peace and blessings be upon him and upon all of them. Isma'il (peace be upon him) had an Arabic tongue but a Syriac lineage, and he is the father of the Arabs who exist today.

His saying ﴿Will you be left in what is here?﴾ is a warning to them, meaning: Do you expect to remain in blessings while you persist in your disobedience? "Al-hadim" means soft and moist. "Al-tal'" is the kafra, which is the cluster of the palm tree before it emerges from its sheath at the beginning of its growth. The implication is that its spathe bears fruit and becomes ripe dates. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: it had ripened and reached maturity while still being hadim. Al-Zuhri said: "Al-hadim" is the soft, delicate thing when it first emerges. Al-Zajjaj said: it is, as has been said, that whose moisture is without a pit. Al-Dahhak said: "Al-hadim" is that whose parts are piled upon one another.

Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak.

The majority read ﴿tanhituna﴾ with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, and he mentioned that this is a dialect. Abu 'Amr said: this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Haywa. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿fari'in﴾, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿fareehin﴾. Mujahid read ﴿mutafarrihin﴾ with a mim, on the pattern of mutafa''ilin. The word is derived from farah, which is the excellence of a thing's appearance and the strength of its perfection in its kind. So the meaning of the verse is: intelligent and attentive. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: exultant and insolent. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad took it to mean: "mustafrihin," that is, those who exaggerate in seeking the excellent of everything from what they make and what they desire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾ addresses the majority of his people, and by "the extravagant" he meant their great men and the leaders of disbelief and misguidance among them.

His saying ﴿among the bewitched﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that it derives from "sihr" (with a kasra on the sin), meaning: you have been bewitched, so you are deluded and do not speak rightly. The second is that it derives from "sihr" (with a fatha on the sin), which is the lung. It is said: "sihr" is the windpipe of the lung and what is attached to it, of liver and other organs. That is, you are a son of Adam like us, and it is not valid for you to be a messenger from God, the Exalted. What follows in the verse strengthens this interpretation. From the same word is the verse of Labid:

"If you ask us what we are, we are sparrows of this creature that is nourished (al-musahhar)."

"Al-tasḥir" is also used for the morning meal, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"......... and we take our morning meal of food and drink."

Then they proposed to him a sign. It is narrated that they proposed the emergence of a she-camel from one of their mountains. Its story in this verse is brief, and it has already passed in full detail. When the she-camel emerged, he said to them: ﴿This is a she-camel; she has a share of water﴾, that is, a portion of the water. Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿lahā shurbun wa-lakum shurbun﴾ with a damma on the shin in both places. The accounts of the coming of the she-camel have already preceded.

"Al-su'": is hamstringing her. He threatened them with punishment for it. The apparent meaning of his command is that he meant in this world. He attributed her hamstringing to all of them, although Qidar al-Ahmar was specifically responsible for hamstringing her, because they agreed upon it in opinion and plan.

His saying ﴿so they became regretful﴾: when the change in their complexions became apparent, in accordance with what Salih (peace be upon him) had told them, they regretted, and they saw that the matter was as he had reported, until the punishment descended upon them. It was a single cry, by which their bodies became rigid and their hearts burst, and they all died, to the last one. Stones were also rained down upon them during that.

﴿Thamud denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Salih said to them: "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft?﴾ ﴿And you carve out homes from the mountains, skillfully.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant,﴾ ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ ﴿They said: "You are only one of those bewitched.﴾ ﴿You are only a human like us, so bring a sign if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of a known day.﴾ ﴿Do not touch her with harm, lest the punishment of a tremendous day seize you."﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, and so they became regretful.﴾ ﴿Then the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

"Thamud": an Arab tribe. It is read both with and without tanwin (nunation), depending on whether the intended meaning is the clan or the tribe. It was recited in both ways: the majority read it without tanwin, while Ibn Wathhab and others read it with tanwin. "Salih" was their brother by lineage. The prophets from among the Arabs are four: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, and Muhammad (ﷺ), may God's peace and blessings be upon him and upon all of them. Isma'il (peace be upon him) had an Arabic tongue but a Syriac lineage, and he is the father of the Arabs who exist today.

His saying ﴿Will you be left in what is here?﴾ is a warning to them, meaning: Do you expect to remain in blessings while you persist in your disobedience? "Al-hadim" means soft and moist. "Al-tal'" is the kafra, which is the cluster of the palm tree before it emerges from its sheath at the beginning of its growth. The implication is that its spathe bears fruit and becomes ripe dates. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: it had ripened and reached maturity while still being hadim. Al-Zuhri said: "Al-hadim" is the soft, delicate thing when it first emerges. Al-Zajjaj said: it is, as has been said, that whose moisture is without a pit. Al-Dahhak said: "Al-hadim" is that whose parts are piled upon one another.

Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak.

The majority read ﴿tanhituna﴾ with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, and he mentioned that this is a dialect. Abu 'Amr said: this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Haywa. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿fari'in﴾, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿fareehin﴾. Mujahid read ﴿mutafarrihin﴾ with a mim, on the pattern of mutafa''ilin. The word is derived from farah, which is the excellence of a thing's appearance and the strength of its perfection in its kind. So the meaning of the verse is: intelligent and attentive. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: exultant and insolent. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad took it to mean: "mustafrihin," that is, those who exaggerate in seeking the excellent of everything from what they make and what they desire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾ addresses the majority of his people, and by "the extravagant" he meant their great men and the leaders of disbelief and misguidance among them.

His saying ﴿among the bewitched﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that it derives from "sihr" (with a kasra on the sin), meaning: you have been bewitched, so you are deluded and do not speak rightly. The second is that it derives from "sihr" (with a fatha on the sin), which is the lung. It is said: "sihr" is the windpipe of the lung and what is attached to it, of liver and other organs. That is, you are a son of Adam like us, and it is not valid for you to be a messenger from God, the Exalted. What follows in the verse strengthens this interpretation. From the same word is the verse of Labid:

"If you ask us what we are, we are sparrows of this creature that is nourished (al-musahhar)."

"Al-tasḥir" is also used for the morning meal, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"......... and we take our morning meal of food and drink."

Then they proposed to him a sign. It is narrated that they proposed the emergence of a she-camel from one of their mountains. Its story in this verse is brief, and it has already passed in full detail. When the she-camel emerged, he said to them: ﴿This is a she-camel; she has a share of water﴾, that is, a portion of the water. Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿lahā shurbun wa-lakum shurbun﴾ with a damma on the shin in both places. The accounts of the coming of the she-camel have already preceded.

"Al-su'": is hamstringing her. He threatened them with punishment for it. The apparent meaning of his command is that he meant in this world. He attributed her hamstringing to all of them, although Qidar al-Ahmar was specifically responsible for hamstringing her, because they agreed upon it in opinion and plan.

His saying ﴿so they became regretful﴾: when the change in their complexions became apparent, in accordance with what Salih (peace be upon him) had told them, they regretted, and they saw that the matter was as he had reported, until the punishment descended upon them. It was a single cry, by which their bodies became rigid and their hearts burst, and they all died, to the last one. Stones were also rained down upon them during that.

His saying ﴿Will you be left in what is here?﴾ is a warning to them, meaning: Do you expect to remain in blessings while you persist in your disobedience? "Al-hadim" means soft and moist. "Al-tal'" is the kafra, which is the cluster of the palm tree before it emerges from its sheath at the beginning of its growth. The implication is that its spathe bears fruit and becomes ripe dates. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: it had ripened and reached maturity while still being hadim. Al-Zuhri said: "Al-hadim" is the soft, delicate thing when it first emerges. Al-Zajjaj said: it is, as has been said, that whose moisture is without a pit. Al-Dahhak said: "Al-hadim" is that whose parts are piled upon one another.

Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak.

The majority read ﴿tanhituna﴾ with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, and he mentioned that this is a dialect. Abu 'Amr said: this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Haywa. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿fari'in﴾, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿fareehin﴾. Mujahid read ﴿mutafarrihin﴾ with a mim, on the pattern of mutafa''ilin. The word is derived from farah, which is the excellence of a thing's appearance and the strength of its perfection in its kind. So the meaning of the verse is: intelligent and attentive. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: exultant and insolent. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad took it to mean: "mustafrihin," that is, those who exaggerate in seeking the excellent of everything from what they make and what they desire.

The first is that it derives from "sihr" (with a kasra on the sin), meaning: you have been bewitched, so you are deluded and do not speak rightly. The second is that it derives from "sihr" (with a fatha on the sin), which is the lung. It is said: "sihr" is the windpipe of the lung and what is attached to it, of liver and other organs. "......... and we take our morning meal of food and drink."

Its story in this verse is brief, and it has already passed in full detail. Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿lahā shurbun wa-lakum shurbun﴾ with a damma on the shin in both places. The accounts of the coming of the she-camel have already preceded.

He attributed her hamstringing to all of them, although Qidar al-Ahmar was specifically responsible for hamstringing her, because they agreed upon it in opinion and plan.

His saying ﴿so they became regretful﴾: when the change in their complexions became apparent, in accordance with what Salih (peace be upon him) had told them, they regretted, and they saw that the matter was as he had reported, until the punishment descended upon them. It was a single cry, by which their bodies became rigid and their hearts burst, and they all died, to the last one. Stones were also rained down upon them during that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verse 200–209:

His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿It will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive.﴾ ﴿Then they will say, "Will we be reprieved?"﴾ ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ ﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy for years,﴾ ﴿then there comes to them that which they were promised,﴾ ﴿what they were given enjoyment of will not avail them?﴾ ﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had warners,﴾ ﴿as a reminder; and We are not unjust.﴾

The reference of "Thus" (dhalika) is to what results for the hearer of the preceding verses from the decree upon them that they will not believe, and that is His saying: ﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 198], the verse. "Salaknahu" (We caused it to enter) means "We made it enter," and the pronoun in it refers to the disbelief implied by His saying: ﴿They were not going to believe in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 199]; this was said by al-Hasan. Al-Rummani said: there is no basis for this except that its mention has not preceded, rather the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and its occurrence to the mind. Al-Zahrawi related that the pronoun refers to the implied denial (al-takdhib al-mafhum), and al-Tha'labi related it as well. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verses 217–226:

His, the Mighty, the Merciful, the Exalted said:

﴿And put your trust in the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner﴾ ﴿They listen eagerly, and most of them are liars﴾ ﴿And the poets—those astray follow them﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Shayba recited "fa-tawakkal" with the fa' (فَتُوَكَّلُ), and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Madina and Syria; the majority recite it with the waw (وَتَوَكَّلْ), and likewise in the rest of the codices. He, the Exalted, commanded him to put his trust in Him in all his affairs, then He brought the attributes that comfort the one who trusts, namely might and mercy, which are mentioned at the end of the stories of the nations mentioned in this surah, and it includes the victory of every prophet over the disbelievers, the concern for his affair, and regard for him.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾, it is an expression for perception. The apparent meaning of the verse is the standing for prayer, and it is possible that it means all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatada. As for His saying: ﴿among those who prostrate﴾, i.e., among the people of prayer, meaning your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and others. Mujahid also said: the turning of your eyes and sights among those who prostrate when you see them from behind your back.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And this meaning is foreign here.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Qatada also said: He meant your turning among the believers, so He expressed them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: He meant the prophets, i.e., your turning as you turn other prophets.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾, here is a question and a demand for affirmation. "Al-affak" (الأفّاك) means the liar, and "al-athim" (الأثِيم) means the sinner. He means the soothsayers (kahana), because they would receive from the devils one word that had been heard from the heaven, and they would mix with it a hundred lies. When that word came true, it became a cause of misguidance for whoever heard it. His saying "yulqun" (يُلْقُونَ) refers to the devils, and it follows from this that the eavesdropping devil also used to lie in addition to what he heard; this is in most cases. It is possible that the pronoun in "yulqun" (i.e., they lie) refers to the soothsayers.

When he mentioned the soothsayers with their falsehood and lying, which entails negating their speech from the speech of Allah, the Exalted, he followed that with the mention of the poets and their condition, to draw attention to the distance of their speech from the speech of Allah, the Exalted, in the Qur'an, since some of the disbelievers said of the Qur'an that it is poetry. This allusion is to the poetry of the Jahiliyya. Al-Naqqash related from al-Suddi that it refers to Ibn al-Zib'ara, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Abu 'Izza, and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first two of them repented and believed, may Allah be pleased with them both. Every mixed poet who satirizes or praises for desire, slanders chaste women, and speaks falsehood enters into the verse.

Nafi' recited "yatba'uhum" (يَتْبَعُهُمْ) with a sukun on the ta' and a fatha on the ba', and this is the recitation of Abu 'Abdullah and al-Hasan (in one report from him). The rest recited it with a shadda on the ta' and a kasra on the ba' (يَتَّبِعُهُمُ).

People differed concerning His saying "al-ghawun" (الغاوُونَ). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they are the narrators (ruwat). He also said: they are those who admire their poetry and keep company with them. 'Ikrima said: they are the rabble who follow the poet, and this is the most preferred of the opinions. Mujahid and Qatada said: "al-ghawun" are the devils. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In every valley they wander﴾ is an expression for their confusion and their plunging into every kind of worthless and false speech, and their adorning of the ugly and disparaging of the beautiful, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾ mentions their indulgence and their going to extremes in the figurative use of speech until it leads to falsehood. However, in this expression there is an excuse for some of them at times. It is related that when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi over Maysan, and he said the famous verse to his wife, 'Umar removed him, and he argued against him with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾, so 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, averted the prescribed punishment for wine from him. Jabir ibn 'Abdullah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: «Whoever walks seven steps in poetry is written among the ghawin», mentioned by Asad ibn Musa, and mentioned by al-Naqqash.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 26, verse 227:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, and remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will come to know what [sort of] return they will be returned to.﴾

This exception concerns the poets of Islam, such as Hassan ibn Thabit, Ka'b ibn Malik, and 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha, and everyone who is characterized by this attribute. It is narrated from 'Ata' ibn Yasar that these [poets] were distressed by what had been mentioned earlier concerning poetry, so they mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and a verse was revealed making an exception for poetry.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and remember Allah often﴾, it may mean: in their poetry; this is the interpretation of Ibn Zayd. It may also mean: that [remembrance] is their disposition, their habit, and their worship; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is like what Labid said when he was asked for poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it." Every poet in Islam who satirizes or praises without right, and does not refrain from base speech, is included in this verse; and every pious one among them who remembers Allah much and refrains from whatever is blameworthy is included in the exception. His saying: "and defend themselves" refers to what they said of poetry and other than it concerning the Quraysh. Qatada said: "and defend themselves with the same as they were wronged."

The remainder of the verse is a warning to the wrongdoers, the disbelievers of Makkah, and a threat to them. The word "yanqalibuna" (they will be returned) functions as the governing verb for "ayy" (which) because it is placed after it. Power and strength belong to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, knows best.

Completed by the praise and success of Allah is the tafsir of Surat ash-Shu'ara'.

And may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
